name: Longevity / Blue Zones diets

lead: Blue Zones diets copy the largely plant-based eating of places such as Sardinia, Okinawa and Nicoya, where residents are reported to live unusually long.
They appear in longevity and appearance discussions. Reviewers note no controlled studies and have challenged the accuracy of the age data.

paras: The idea is that plant-heavy food, activity, low stress and social ties together support long life; the diet's separate contribution has not been tested.
No specific harms are documented; critics focus on weak evidence and commercial packaging of the concept.

lead: Blue Zones diets are eating patterns modelled on regions reported to have unusually many long-lived people: Sardinia, Okinawa, Nicoya in Costa Rica, Icaria in Greece, and later Martinique [1]. They are generally described as predominantly plant-based, alongside physical activity, low stress and social ties [1].

The idea originated in a 1999 Sardinia study and a 2004 follow-up by Michel Poulain, Gianni Pes and colleagues; Dan Buettner popularised it from 2005 and Blue Zones LLC was formed in 2008 [1]. In looksmaxxing and longevity circles these diets are cited as a model for healthy aging and skin. Critics have questioned the age data, and reviews report no controlled trials of the diets [1].

paras: The 1999 Sardinia study reported 13 centenarians per 100,000 people, and the 2004 AKEA study located the concentration in mountain villages of Nuoro Province. The name reportedly came from marking villages on a map with a blue pen [1].
A predominantly plant-based diet is listed among the factors under research, together with physical activity, low stress and social interaction. A 2013 review also cited locally produced food [1].
No studies found. A 2021 review by Harriet Hall noted there are no controlled studies of elderly people in the blue zones, and called diet claims speculative [1].

Studies have been challenged for not validating ages and relying on unreliable records. Okinawa's family registers were largely destroyed in 1945 and later reconstructed, and Okinawa's advantage declined in the 21st century [1]. A 2024 Science review by Ignacio Amigo found no scientific evidence linking community lifestyle to longevity [1]. Austad and Pes (2025) defended the demographic work [1].

lore.intro: Online, the diets are cited as a template for aging well; the source material for community claims is limited.

claims.claim: Eating like Blue Zone residents extends lifespan.
The diets keep skin and appearance youthful.

timeline.event: AKEA study identifies longevity in Nuoro villages [1].
